content.title: Tems steals Coachella night 2 in the Justin Bieber set
content.text: The Grammy-winning Nigerian artist joined Justin Bieber on stage at Coachella 2026. Nobody in the crowd at the Empire Polo Club on Saturday night was prepared for what the final stretch of Justin Bieber’s set would deliver. After a 90-minute performance that ranged from raw and intimate to nostalgia-soaked and chaotic, Bieber invited Tems onto the stage, and the energy shifted in a way that only she can produce. The Lagos-born singer, born Temilade Openiyi, has spent the last several years quietly building one of the most remarkable trajectories in contemporary music. Two Grammy Awards. A record-breaking 40 million monthly listeners on Spotify, the first Nigerian artist to reach that milestone. Collaborations with Drake, Beyoncé and Bieber himself. Saturday night at Coachella was not her first brush with a crowd of this size, but it was a reminder of what makes her singular. She appeared first for I Think You’re Special, a song that showcased the gentle authority she carries into every room she enters. Then she stayed. Wizkid joined them both for Essence, a track that originally introduced Tems to a global audience back in 2020, and the full-circle weight of that moment was not lost on anyone watching. How she got here Tems launched her career in 2018 with her debut single Mr Rebel, recording it after leaving a full-time job to pursue music. For two years, she worked in relative obscurity. Then Wizkid called. Their 2020 collaboration Essence became a slow-burning phenomenon, crossing from Lagos to London to Los Angeles in a way that few Afrobeats records had done before it. The song reached the Billboard Hot 100, earned a remix featuring Justin Bieber, and opened doors that she has never stopped walking through. What followed was a run of features and solo work that placed her alongside the biggest names in the industry. She appeared on Drake’s Certified Lover Boy, contributed to Beyoncé’s Renaissance, and released her own debut album If Orange Was a Colour, which confirmed that her voice was not a feature act waiting for a solo career. It already had one. The woman behind the voice In a recent interview, Tems spoke openly about the personal changes that have come with her rise. Before music, she described herself as someone who pushed people away, someone whose independence had become a wall rather than a strength. The process of making art and sharing it publicly, she said, taught her to open up in ways she had not expected. That vulnerability is audible in her work. Her voice carries a weight that most singers spend entire careers chasing, a low, textured tone that does not perform emotion so much as inhabit it. On the Coachella stage on Saturday, standing next to one of the most famous pop stars on earth, she did not compete for the room. She simply existed in it, and the room came to her. What the Coachella moment means Bieber’s set had its uneven stretches. The production was minimal for a headlining performance, and a long run of material from his album Swag tested the patience of a crowd hungry for the hits. He recovered with a disarming laptop session, playing old music videos and singing along to songs he had not touched in over a decade, asking the crowd before each one how far back they should go By the time Tems appeared, the night had already found its footing. Her presence sharpened it into something more significant. The collaboration between two artists who grew up on opposite sides of the Atlantic, who found each other through a remix and kept finding reasons to share a stage, landed with the kind of quiet impact that does not need fireworks to register. Tems has said she has been dreaming about this kind of moment for a long time. On Saturday night at Coachella, it looked less like a dream and more like a destination she had been walking toward all along.
